name: Vicar
milestone_by_age_26: Won a drawing competition in 1957 and became a professional cartoonist creating multiple published comic strips for major Chilean newspapers and magazines including El Mercurio, Barrabases, and Topaze by age 26.
early_history_summary: Trained as an electronics engineer at the Technical State University of Chile, Vicar won a drawing competition in 1957 at age 23 and pivoted to a cartooning career. He created comic strips such as Locutín, Hipólito y Camilo, Quevedo, and Paquita for Chilean publications including El Mercurio's Mampato supplement, Barrabases, El Pingüino, and Topaze throughout the late 1950s.
family_context_summary: Trained as an electronics engineer at the Technical State University of Chile; design jobs financially supported his university studies. Not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Vicar was trained as an electronics engineer but pivoted to cartooning after winning a drawing competition in 1957 at age 23. He quickly established himself with comic strips in major Chilean publications like El Mercurio and Barrabases. No family background in art or cartooning is documented. His early advantage was largely self-created through direct domain exposure and persistent practice in Chilean print media.
starting_point: Born in Santiago, Chile in 1934; trained as an electronics engineer at the Technical State University of Chile, with design jobs funding his studies.
current_position: Died on January 3, 2012 at age 77 in Santiago, Chile; final role: prolific Disney comics artist and founder of Vic-Art studio.

trajectory.event: Won a drawing competition and began professional cartooning career with comic strips in Chilean newspapers.
Moved to Barcelona, Spain and joined Bardon Art studios to pursue international illustration work.
Began drawing Disney comics for Danish publisher Gutenberghus (Egmont), launching his most famous career phase.
Returned to Chile and founded Vic-Art studio with multiple artists and inkers.
Died on January 3, 2012 in Santiago after a long battle with leukemia.

name: Mirko Bašić
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic gold medal with Yugoslavia at the 1984 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles as starting goalkeeper, playing all six matches.
early_history_summary: Bašić debuted for RK Partizan Bjelovar at age 16 in 1976 and developed into one of the top goalkeepers in Yugoslav handball. He moved to RK Metaloplastika Šabac in 1980, where he became a key player in the club that dominated European handball in the 1980s.
family_context_summary: Born in Bjelovar, FPR Yugoslavia (now Croatia). Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Bašić debuted professionally at 16 for Partizan Bjelovar and joined RK Metaloplastika Šabac at 20, entering the elite Yugoslav handball pipeline that produced the dominant European club of the 1980s. His physical talent as a goalkeeper was recognized early, and the Yugoslav sports system provided a structured performance pipeline. Family background is not documented. By 24, he was Olympic gold medalist and starting goalkeeper for Yugoslavia.
starting_point: Born in Bjelovar, FPR Yugoslavia (now Croatia) in 1960; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Retired from professional handball; last known role as assistant coach with Croatian national teams; father of professional handball player Sonja Bašić.

trajectory.event: Debuted for RK Partizan Bjelovar as a teenage goalkeeper.
Joined RK Metaloplastika Šabac, the club that would dominate European handball in the 1980s.
Won Olympic gold medal with Yugoslavia at the Los Angeles Olympics, playing all six matches as goalkeeper.
Won the European Champions Cup with RK Metaloplastika.
Won a second consecutive European Champions Cup with RK Metaloplastika.
Won Olympic bronze medal with Yugoslavia at the Seoul Olympics.
Won the Cup Winners' Cup with OM Vitrolles in France.

name: Javier Zanetti
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1998 UEFA Cup with Inter Milan, scoring the second goal in a 3-0 final victory over Lazio, and had already earned a starting role at a top European club and multiple Argentina national team caps by age 26.
early_history_summary: Rejected by Independiente's youth academy at 16 for being too small, Zanetti joined second-division Talleres in 1991, then moved to Banfield in the first division in 1993, debuting at age 20. His performances earned a national team call-up at 21 and a transfer to Inter Milan in 1995 at age 22, where he became an immediate starter.
primary_leverage_engine: Physical stamina and relentless work ethic
family_context_summary: Born in Buenos Aires, Argentina; father Rodolfo was a bricklayer and Zanetti worked delivering milk and as an assistant bricklayer in his youth. Working-class background.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; no evidence of family involvement in professional football.
evidence_summary: Zanetti grew up in a working-class family in Buenos Aires, delivering milk and helping his bricklayer father before pursuing football. Rejected by Independiente at 16 for being too small, he climbed through the lower divisions to reach Banfield's first team at 20, earned a national team call-up at 21, and transferred to Inter Milan at 22. His path was defined by relentless work ethic and resilience rather than family advantages or inherited networks.
starting_point: Born in Buenos Aires, Argentina in 1973 to a working-class family; father was a bricklayer, and Javier delivered milk and assisted as a bricklayer in his youth.
current_position: Vice-president of Inter Milan; retired as the most decorated player in Inter's history with 16 trophies and 858 appearances; Argentina's most-capped player with 145 caps.

trajectory.event: Debuted for Banfield in Argentina's first division and scored his first goal 17 days later.
Earned his first Argentina national team call-up under coach Daniel Passarella.

Won the UEFA Cup with Inter Milan, scoring the second goal in a 3-0 final victory over Lazio.
Won the Champions League with Inter Milan under Jose Mourinho, completing a historic treble.
Retired from professional football after 858 appearances for Inter Milan.

name: Marcus Schenkenberg
milestone_by_age_26: Landed the landmark Calvin Klein advertising campaign in 1991, including a 116-page Vanity Fair spread shot by Bruce Weber, establishing him as the first male supermodel.
early_history_summary: Schenkenberg moved from Sweden to the United States in 1987 at age 19, working various jobs including as a nanny in the Hollywood Hills. He was discovered by photographer Barry King on Venice Beach in 1989 while roller-skating, which led to representation and runway work in Milan and Paris before the breakthrough Calvin Klein campaign in 1991.
primary_leverage_engine: Physical appearance and natural camera presence
family_context_summary: Born in Stockholm, Sweden to mixed Dutch-Indonesian parentage. Studied economics in Sweden before moving to the US. Family financial background not documented.
evidence_summary: Schenkenberg was discovered casually on Venice Beach in 1989 at age 21 while working as a nanny, with no prior modeling training or family connections in fashion. His striking physical appearance (6'4" with distinctive features) was the primary catalyst. The 1991 Calvin Klein campaign shot by Bruce Weber launched him as the first male supermodel, riding the 1990s supermodel cultural wave. No family advantages or domain connections are documented.
starting_point: Born in Stockholm, Sweden in 1968 to mixed Dutch-Indonesian parents; studied economics in Sweden before moving to the United States in 1987.
current_position: Continues to model and make television appearances; represented by Kuhlmann Consulting Group and minor Ford Models; widely regarded as the first male supermodel.

trajectory.event: Discovered by photographer Barry King on Venice Beach, Los Angeles, while roller-skating.
Landed the landmark Calvin Klein campaign shot by Bruce Weber for Vanity Fair, establishing him as the first male supermodel.
Published book 'Marcus Schenkenberg: New Rules' and expanded into television and music.
Appeared on VH1's The Surreal Life and continued international TV appearances.

name: Anish Kapoor
milestone_by_age_26: Held his first solo exhibition at Patrice Alexandre in Paris in 1980, presenting the groundbreaking pigment-coated sculpture series '1000 Names' that first garnered serious international attention.
early_history_summary: Born in Mumbai to a Jewish mother and Indian Hindu father, Kapoor attended the elite Doon School before briefly studying electrical engineering in Israel. He moved to London in 1973, studied at Hornsey College of Art and Chelsea School of Art, and was mentored by Romanian sculptor Paul Neagu. After graduating, he taught at Wolverhampton Polytechnic and developed his signature pigment sculptures following a transformative trip to India in 1979.
family_context_summary: Born in Mumbai to a Jewish mother of Iraqi origin and an Indian Punjabi Hindu father who was a hydrographer and applied physicist serving in the Indian Navy. Attended The Doon School, an elite boarding school.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a hydrographer and applied physicist in the Indian Navy; maternal grandfather was cantor of a synagogue in Pune. No direct art-world family connections documented.
evidence_summary: Kapoor benefited from an elite educational path: The Doon School in India, then Hornsey College of Art and Chelsea School of Art in London, where mentor Paul Neagu shaped his sculptural approach. His father's naval career provided a middle-class-to-upper background supporting international education. The London art school ecosystem of the 1970s, with access to Lisson Gallery artists like Donald Judd, provided critical network density. His first solo show in Paris in 1980 at age 26 launched his international career.
starting_point: Born in Mumbai, India in 1954 to a Jewish mother of Iraqi origin and an Indian Punjabi Hindu father who was a hydrographer and applied physicist in the Indian Navy; attended the elite Doon School boarding school.
current_position: Sir Anish Kapoor CBE RA; one of the world's most prominent sculptors; lives and works in London and Venice; estimated net worth in the tens of millions.

trajectory.event: Held first solo exhibition at Patrice Alexandre in Paris, presenting the '1000 Names' pigment sculpture series.
First solo exhibition at Lisson Gallery, London, and Artist in Residence at Walker Art Gallery, Liverpool.
Represented Britain at the Venice Biennale and won the Premio Duemila Prize.
Won the Turner Prize at the Tate Gallery, London.
Appointed CBE for services to the arts.
Became the first living artist to have a solo exhibition at the Royal Academy of Arts, London.

name: Seyran Ateş
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone in her professional domain (law) by age 26 found. She published an autobiography at 17 and was shot in 1984 at age 21 while working at a women's center, but did not begin practicing law until 1997 at age 34. Her major recognition came later.
early_history_summary: Born in Istanbul to a Turkish mother and Kurdish father, Ateş moved to West Berlin at age 6. She left home at 17 to avoid an arranged marriage and published her first autobiography that year. She began studying law at the Free University of Berlin in 1983 but was shot in the neck in 1984 at a women's center, interrupting her studies for six years. She resumed law studies in 1990 and qualified as a lawyer in 1997.
family_context_summary: Born in Istanbul to a Turkish mother and Kurdish father; family moved to West Berlin when she was 6 as part of the Turkish guest worker migration. Grew up in a conservative Sunni Muslim family.

name: Sylvia Plath
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Mademoiselle national college fiction contest in 1952 with a $500 prize and publication, followed by a prestigious guest editorship at Mademoiselle magazine in New York in 1953, establishing her as a recognized young literary talent by age 21.
early_history_summary: Plath published her first poem at age 8 in the Boston Herald and continued publishing in regional magazines throughout her teens. At 17, just after graduating high school, she had her first national publication in The Christian Science Monitor. At Smith College she excelled academically, won the Mademoiselle fiction contest at 20, served as guest editor at Mademoiselle in 1953, graduated summa cum laude in 1955, and won a Fulbright Scholarship to Cambridge.
primary_leverage_engine: Intense literary ambition and early publication
family_context_summary: Born in Jamaica Plain, Boston; father Otto Plath was a professor of biology and entomology at Boston University; mother Aurelia was a teacher who had been Otto's student. Upper-middle-class academic family. Father died when Sylvia was 8, creating financial strain.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an entomologist and professor at Boston University who authored a book on bumblebees; mother was a high school teacher. Both parents valued learning and encouraged intellectual excellence.
evidence_summary: Plath grew up in an academic household with a Boston University professor father and teacher mother, both of whom valued learning intensely. She began publishing poetry at age 8 and maintained relentless output through her teens. Smith College provided an elite institutional platform where she won a national fiction contest at 20 and a Mademoiselle guest editorship at 21. Her father's death at 8 introduced both financial strain and psychological adversity that fueled her confessional writing style. The combination of early literary reps, academic infrastructure, and intense concentration on craft produced a major literary voice by her early twenties.
starting_point: Born in 1932 in Boston, Massachusetts to an academic family; father was a biology professor at Boston University and mother was a teacher; grew up in the upper-middle-class suburb of Wellesley after father's death in 1940.
current_position: Died on February 11, 1963 at age 30 in London, England; final role: poet and novelist, author of The Colossus and The Bell Jar; posthumously awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1982.

trajectory.event: First national publication in The Christian Science Monitor and first story published in Seventeen magazine.
Won Mademoiselle magazine's national college fiction contest with a $500 prize and publication.
Served as guest editor at Mademoiselle magazine in New York for the August college issue.
Graduated summa cum laude from Smith College and awarded a Fulbright Scholarship to Cambridge University.
Married English poet Ted Hughes on June 16, 1956 in London.
Published her first poetry collection, The Colossus, in England.
Published The Bell Jar under the pseudonym Victoria Lucas; died by suicide on February 11, 1963.

name: Erik Schinegger
milestone_by_age_26: Won the women's downhill world championship title at the 1966 FIS Alpine World Ski Championships in Portillo, Chile, at age 18, becoming a world champion skier.
early_history_summary: Born in Agsdorf, Carinthia, Austria and raised as a girl named Erika, Schinegger made skis from barrel staves at age 8 and won a race from an impossible 314th starting position at age 12. Invited to the Austrian National Youth Team at 16, he became a European junior champion in 1965 and rapidly rose to win the downhill world championship at 18 in 1966.
family_context_summary: Born to a prosperous farming family in Austria's Carinthia mountains, home to future champion downhiller Franz Klammer. Grew up helping with farm chores in a rural alpine setting.
parent_family_domain_summary: Farming family in the Austrian Alps; no direct family connection to ski racing documented, but geographic proximity to alpine skiing culture was inherent.
evidence_summary: Schinegger grew up in the Austrian Alps on a prosperous farm, immersed in alpine skiing culture from childhood. He made his own skis from barrel staves at 8 and won races from impossibly early starting positions as a child. The Austrian national ski team pipeline absorbed him at 16, providing elite coaching, equipment (Kneissl sponsorship), and competition access. His physical talent was noted as he occasionally clocked times better than male skiers. The combination of geographic immersion, early specialization, and the Austrian ski system produced a world champion by 18.
starting_point: Born in Agsdorf, Carinthia, Austria in 1948 to a prosperous farming family in the alpine mountains; raised as a girl named Erika due to intersex condition unrecognized at birth.
current_position: Owner of a children's ski school and two inns in his hometown of Agsdorf, Carinthia, Austria; married with a daughter and two grandsons.

trajectory.event: Won the European junior championship in downhill skiing and was invited to the Austrian National Youth Team.

Medical examination before the Grenoble Olympics revealed he was genetically male; withdrew from women's racing and transitioned.
Married and became father of a daughter; later established a children's ski school in Carinthia.

name: Aleksandar Matanović
milestone_by_age_26: Awarded the Grandmaster title by FIDE in 1955 at age 25, recognizing him as one of the leading Yugoslav chess players, having already won the Yugoslav Junior Championship in 1948 and earned the International Master title in 1951.
early_history_summary: Matanović learned chess at age 6 from his sister in Belgrade. He became Youth Champion of Serbia in 1947 at age 17, Youth Champion of Yugoslavia in 1948, earned the National Master title in 1949, International Master in 1951, and Grandmaster in 1955. He was a permanent member of the Yugoslav Olympic team from 1954 onward.
family_context_summary: Born in Belgrade, Yugoslavia; learned chess at age 6 from his sister. Family background beyond this not documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Sister taught him chess at age 6, indicating some family familiarity with the game, but no professional chess background documented.
evidence_summary: Matanović learned chess from his sister at age 6 in Belgrade and rapidly progressed through Yugoslavia's strong chess ecosystem, winning junior championships as a teenager and earning master titles in quick succession. The Yugoslav chess infrastructure of the 1940s-50s was one of the world's strongest, providing elite competition and team opportunities. His early specialization and sustained practice from childhood produced a Grandmaster title by 25. No significant family financial or domain advantages are documented beyond his sister's early introduction.
starting_point: Born in Belgrade, Yugoslavia in 1930; learned chess at age 6 from his sister; family background not documented beyond this.
current_position: Died on August 9, 2023 at age 93 in Belgrade, Serbia; final role: chess grandmaster, co-founder of Chess Informant, and former FIDE Vice President.

trajectory.event: Became Youth Champion of Serbia in chess.

name: Rafael Frühbeck de Burgos
milestone_by_age_26: Appointed principal conductor of the Bilbao Symphony Orchestra in 1958 at age 25, after graduating summa cum laude from the Munich Hochschule für Musik and winning the Richard Strauss Prize.
early_history_summary: Born in Burgos, Spain to German parents, Frühbeck's mother introduced him to the violin at age 7. He became concertmaster of the local orchestra by 14 and was conducting a zarzuela company at 16. After studying at conservatories in Bilbao and Madrid, he undertook military service directing a military band, then studied conducting at the Munich Hochschule für Musik, graduating summa cum laude and winning the Richard Strauss Prize before returning to Spain in 1958.
primary_leverage_engine: Early musical training and conducting immersion
family_context_summary: Born in Burgos, Spain to German parents; father was a businessman wounded in WWI who settled in Spain working for a German company. Mother was an arts enthusiast who introduced him to the violin at age 7. Sent to the German School in Barcelona.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother was an arts enthusiast who bought him his first violin and nurtured his early musical education. Father was a businessman, not a musician, but the family's German cultural heritage provided exposure to classical music traditions.
evidence_summary: Frühbeck de Burgos benefited from a culturally rich German-Spanish household where his mother introduced him to the violin at 7 and sent him to the German School in Barcelona. He was concertmaster by 14 and conducting by 16, showing prodigy-level early musical development. The conservatory pipeline in Bilbao, Madrid, and Munich provided elite training, while military service as a band director gave him orchestral transcription experience. His mother's arts enthusiasm and the family's German cultural heritage were the primary early advantages, supplemented by formal institutional training.
starting_point: Born in Burgos, Spain in 1933 to German parents; father was a businessman wounded in WWI who settled in Spain, mother was an arts enthusiast who introduced him to the violin at age 7.
current_position: Died on June 11, 2014 at age 80 in Pamplona, Spain; final role: chief conductor of the Danish National Symphony Orchestra and renowned guest conductor at major orchestras worldwide.

name: Pedro Martínez
milestone_by_age_26: Won the National League Cy Young Award in 1997 at age 26 with a 17-8 record, NL-best 1.90 ERA, 13 complete games, and 305 strikeouts for the Montreal Expos, cementing his status as one of baseball's elite pitchers.
early_history_summary: Born in extreme poverty in Manoguayabo, Dominican Republic, Martínez grew up in a one-room palm wood house with dirt floors. He signed with the Los Angeles Dodgers for $6,000 at age 16 in 1988, following his older brother Ramón who was already a Dodgers pitcher. He dominated the minor leagues, reached MLB at 20 in 1992, had a strong 1993 relief season (10-5, 2.61 ERA), was traded to Montreal in 1994, made his first All-Star team in 1996, and won the Cy Young in 1997.
family_context_summary: Born into extreme poverty in Manoguayabo, Dominican Republic; fifth of six siblings in a palm wood house with dirt floors and a tin roof. Father worked odd jobs and was a former amateur baseball player; mother washed clothes for wealthy families. Parents divorced when he was 9.
parent_family_domain_summary: Older brother Ramón Martínez signed with the Dodgers in 1984 and became a 20-game winner, creating a direct family pipeline to professional baseball. Father was a former amateur baseball player. Three of the Martínez brothers became professional pitchers.
evidence_summary: Martínez grew up in extreme poverty in the Dominican Republic but benefited from a critical family pipeline: his older brother Ramón was already a Dodgers star pitcher who paved the way for Pedro's signing at 16. The Dodgers' Dominican scouting infrastructure and minor league system provided the elite performance pipeline. His father's amateur baseball background and three pitching brothers created a family-domain advantage. Poverty and small stature (5'11", under 150 lbs) created adversity that fueled his competitive intensity. By 26, he was a Cy Young winner with 305 strikeouts, overcoming doubts about his size throughout his career.
starting_point: Born in 1971 in Manoguayabo, Dominican Republic to extreme poverty; father worked odd jobs and mother washed clothes for wealthy families; grew up in a one-room palm wood house with dirt floors and a tin roof.
current_position: Retired MLB pitcher (2009); inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 2015 with 91.1% on first ballot; runs the Pedro Martínez and Brothers Foundation; resides in the Dominican Republic.

trajectory.event: Signed with the Los Angeles Dodgers for $6,000, following older brother Ramón into the organization.

Won the World Series with the Boston Red Sox, ending the franchise's 86-year championship drought.
Inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame on the first ballot with 91.1% of the vote.

name: Tony Parker
milestone_by_age_26: Won his first NBA championship with the San Antonio Spurs in 2003 at age 21, followed by two more titles in 2005 and 2007, and was named NBA Finals MVP in 2007 at age 25, making him one of the most decorated young point guards in NBA history by 26.
early_history_summary: Son of an American professional basketball player who played in Europe, Parker was born in Belgium and raised in France. He began playing organized basketball at age 12 and enrolled at INSEP, France's elite sporting academy, at 15. He turned professional with Paris Basket Racing at 15-16 and was drafted 28th overall by the San Antonio Spurs in the 2001 NBA draft at age 19, becoming the starting point guard within five games.
primary_leverage_engine: Speed and basketball IQ inherited from family
family_context_summary: Born in Bruges, Belgium to Tony Parker Sr., an American professional basketball player who played 15 years in Europe, and Pamela Firestone, a Dutch model. Raised in France following his father's playing contracts. Family immersed in basketball culture from birth.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a professional basketball player (Loyola University Chicago, then 15 years in Europe) who became Tony's first coach and mentor. Two brothers also played basketball at high levels. The family's entire social circle revolved around basketball.
evidence_summary: Parker's career was built on a deep family-domain apprenticeship: his father was a professional basketball player who became his first coach, and the family moved constantly following basketball contracts, immersing Tony in the sport from infancy. France's INSEP sporting academy provided elite training at 15, and Paris Basket Racing gave him professional reps as a teenager. The San Antonio Spurs' system under Gregg Popovich, alongside Tim Duncan and Manu Ginobili, provided the complementary team and elite ecosystem that accelerated his development into a champion by 21.
starting_point: Born in Bruges, Belgium in 1982 to an American professional basketball player father and a Dutch model mother; raised in France following father's European basketball career, immersed in basketball culture from birth.
current_position: Majority owner and head coach of ASVEL Basket in the French LNB Pro A; retired from NBA in 2019 after 18 seasons; inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2023.
